technique.how: Palpate the right lower quadrant, centring on McBurney point (two-thirds of the way from umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine). Note whether tenderness is maximal there and whether it is localized rather than diffuse; also check for pain in the RLQ on left-sided pressure (Rovsing) as a related sign.
technique.prerequisites: Supine, relaxed patient; palpate non-tender areas first.

interpretation.positive_finding: Localized, maximal tenderness at McBurney point substantially raises the odds of appendicitis (OR ~5 in 1,204 patients with RLQ pain); about two-thirds of children with appendicitis have maximal RLQ pain.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of RLQ tenderness lowers the probability of appendicitis but roughly one-third of proven cases (especially retrocaecal, pelvic or early) lack maximal RLQ pain.
interpretation.pitfalls: Cecal diverticulitis, terminal ileitis, ovarian pathology, ectopic pregnancy and mesenteric adenitis all produce RLQ tenderness; the appendix position varies, so pain may be flank, suprapubic or RUQ in pregnancy.
interpretation.changes_what: Present with migration/fever: appendicitis pathway (imaging or surgical review). Absent: lowers suspicion; look for alternative diagnoses but do not stop the work-up if history is typical.

estimates.target_condition: Acute appendicitis (maximal pain in RLQ, pediatric)
estimates.population: 755 children and adolescents with suspected appendicitis, 36% with appendicitis
estimates.computed_from: sensitivity = 1 - 0.32 (proportion of proven appendicitis cases without maximal pain in the RLQ)
estimates.quote: absence of maximal pain in the right lower quadrant (32%)

sources.citation: Kharbanda AB, Taylor GA, Fishman SJ, Bachur RG. Atypical clinical features of pediatric appendicitis. Acad Emerg Med. 2007;14(2):124-129.
Dixon JM, Elton RA, Rainey JB, Macleod DA. Rectal examination in patients with pain in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. BMJ. 1991;302(6773):386-388.
Laurell H, Hansson LE, Gunnarsson U. Manifestations of acute appendicitis: a prospective study on acute abdominal pain. Dig Surg. 2013;30(3):198-206.
Wagner JM, McKinney WP, Carpenter JL. Does this patient have appendicitis? JAMA. 1996;276(19):1589-1594.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of McBurney tenderness to exclude appendicitis in pregnancy, the elderly, or patients with atypical appendix position; do not use in isolation to diagnose in women of reproductive age without pelvic/pregnancy assessment.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: RLQ tenderness with guarding, rigidity, fever or hypotension suggests perforation/abscess: antibiotics, imaging, urgent surgical review.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Localizing tenderness is more reproducible than rebound, but 'maximal' tenderness and its exact site vary between examiners; the OR in Dixon 1991 is unadjusted.

extraction_notes: The Wagner 1996 RCE table (RLQ tenderness pooled sens/spec, LR+ ~7.3-8.5 from memory) is not visible via PubMed/PMC, so it is cited without numbers. Visible numbers: Kharbanda 2007 (pediatric) 32% of proven cases lacked maximal RLQ pain, giving a computed sensitivity of 0.68; Dixon 1991 unadjusted OR 5.09 (odds ratio, stat fields left null); Laurell 2013 OR 3.29 for isolated RIF tenderness (abstract, not entered as a stat). Status partially_quantified; verifier with JAMA access should add the RCE pooled LRs.
